## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action** — including clarifying questions, exploring the codebase, or checking files. If it turns out wrong for the situation, you don't have to use it.

When multiple skills apply, process skills come first — they set the approach, then implementation skills (frontend-design, etc.) carry it out. Brainstorming and systematic-debugging are Superpowers' most common process skills, but the rule holds for any of them.

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |

| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |

| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

</EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>"

commands.name: harness-arc
commands.description: Deploy a large multi-plan design to a Harness fleet as a sequenced chain of PRDs that runs unattended to completion, with a wayfinder map holding the decisions the fleet cannot make; `harness supervise` catches the fleet's silent stall modes. Use when a spec or design is too big for one PRD, when the user wants a fleet to run "fully automatic until shipped", when deploying an implementation plan of several plans/stages, or when asked to watch, babysit, or unstick a running Harness fleet. (user)

commands.name: harness-init
commands.description: First-time Harness setup — run the wizard that writes .harness/config and seeds GitHub labels. Trigger on /harness-init or "set up the harness config". (user)

commands.name: harness-issue

commands.name: harness-one

commands.name: harness-plan

commands.name: harness-prd

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: docs
commands.description: docs (editable docs people share and comment on; the default for any document, named as a doc or not: a document, report, proposal, resume, cover letter, letter, contract, policy, form, template, worksheet, essay, handbook, guide, how-to, cheat sheet, SOP or other writing to keep, share, collaborate on, send, submit, print or sign; a doc exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to pick Word, and a file nobody asked for is a doc, not Word; a plan, comparison, summary or notes asked in chat stays in chat; a pasted claude.ai artifact link may be a doc: check with docs tools first; Word or another file format named, tracked changes wanted, or a .docx to change or use as a template → that format's skill): making one → if no docs-connector instructions are in context, call its `guide` (topic.instructions) first; then create the doc (headings only, no body) before any search, file read or plan, even with files attached. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: import-memory
commands.description: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: morning
commands.description: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: skill-creator
commands.description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx

However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.description: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule.

## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain-text ledger file and is tired of spreadsheets. They need a small, dependency-free Python tool, **pennywise**, that parses that file and reports where the money went — usable both as an importable library (`import pennywise`) and as a `pennywise` terminal command.

## Solution

A pure-stdlib Python ≥3.9 package `pennywise` (src layout, `pyproject.toml` with setuptools, console script `pennywise = pennywise.cli:main`) so `pip install .` gives both the library and the command. A parser turns ledger text into immutable entries; pure functions aggregate/filter them; an `argparse` CLI exposes `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add`, `export`.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I `import pennywise` and call `parse(text)` to get my entries in file order.
2. As a user, I get a `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError`) naming the exact line when my file has a mistake.
3. As a user, I get my balance, totals per category and totals per month from library calls.
4. As a user, I filter entries by category (case-insensitive) and an inclusive date range.
5. As a user, I run `pennywise balance|summary|list FILE` (or `-` for stdin), optionally with `--json`.
6. As a user, I append an entry with `pennywise add` and an invalid entry never touches my file.
7. As a user, I export my ledger as CSV.
8. As a script author, I rely on exit codes 0 / 1 (ledger or entry mistake) / 2 (unreadable file or bad command line).

## Implementation Decisions

Decided by the operator from the brief (unattended run; the brief in `## Original request` wins on any conflict):

- **Layout**: `pyproject.toml` (setuptools build backend, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no dependencies), `src/pennywise/__init__.py` (re-exports `Entry`, `ParseError`, `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`), `src/pennywise/ledger.py` (parsing + aggregation), `src/pennywise/cli.py` (`main(argv=None) -> int`), `src/pennywise/__main__.py` (so `python -m pennywise` works). Tests under `tests/` using stdlib `unittest` (runnable with `python -m unittest` and pytest).
- **Entry**: frozen `dataclass` with `date: datetime.date`, `category: str` (lower case), `amount: Decimal`, `note: str` (`""` when absent).
- **Line handling**: split with `str.splitlines()` (CRLF ok). Line numbers count from 1 including blank/comment lines. A line is blank if it is empty or whitespace-only. A line is a comment if, after stripping leading whitespace, it starts with `#`.
- **Fields**: split on the first three runs of spaces/tabs (`re.split(r"[ \t]+", line.strip(), maxsplit=3)`); fewer than 3 fields is an error. Note = 4th piece (already trimmed at both ends; internal whitespace kept exactly).
- **Date**: must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a real date (`datetime.date(y, m, d)`); `2024-02-30` is an error.
- **Category**: any non-whitespace token, stored with `.lower()`.
- **Amount**: must match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$` (so `12`, `12.5`, `+2500`, `-0.99` ok; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `12.`, `.5` rejected); stored as `Decimal`.
- **ParseError**: subclass of `ValueError`, `.line` = line number, `str()` is `"line N: <reason>"`.
- **Aggregates**: `balance` returns `Decimal("0")` for no entries; `by_category`/`by_month` return plain `dict`s of `Decimal` (month key `"YYYY-MM"`). `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns a new list in input order; category compared case-insensitively; `since`/`until` inclusive.
- **Money formatting** (CLI): `Decimal.quantize(Decimal("0.01"))`, always two decimals; a negative zero prints as `0.00`.
- **CLI output**:
  - `balance`: `1457.50`; `--json` → `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
  - `summary [--by category|month]` (default `category`; any other value → argparse error, exit 2): lines `NAME  TOTAL` (two spaces) sorted by name; `--json` → object with keys sorted by name, string amounts.
  - `list [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]`: entries stably sorted by date (same-day keeps file order), each `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`; `--json` → array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}` objects (note `""` when absent). An invalid `--since`/`--until` date → exit 2.
  - `export [--format csv]`: same order as `list`, written with the `csv` module, header `date,category,amount,note`, `lineterminator="\n"`, amount two decimals. Only `csv` is accepted (other values → exit 2).
  - JSON output via `json.dumps` (default separators) followed by a newline.
- **add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]**: validates the new entry by parsing the composed line with the same parser (DATE, AMOUNT, CATEGORY must be single tokens; NOTE must not contain a newline; CATEGORY must not start with `#`). Invalid → message naming the problem on stderr (mentioning `line 1` style is not required for `add`; it must say what was wrong), exit 1, file byte-for-byte unchanged (and not created). Valid → appends the formatted line (same format as `list`, category lower-cased, amount two decimals) followed by `\n`; if the existing file is non-empty and does not end with a newline, a `\n` is written first. Creates the file if missing. Prints the added line. The existing file content is not validated by `add`. An unreadable/unwritable target → exit 2.
- **Input**: files read as UTF-8; `-` reads `sys.stdin`. Missing/unreadable file (including a directory) → `pennywise: <reason>` on stderr, exit 2.
- **Errors**: a ParseError → `pennywise: line N: <reason>` on stderr, nothing on stdout, exit 1. Output is fully computed before anything is printed, so a failure never leaves partial stdout. No command / unknown command / bad option → argparse usage error, exit 2.

## Testing Decisions

- Unit tests for the parser: every valid/invalid amount from the brief, the impossible date, blank/comment lines and line numbering, tabs and multiple spaces, notes with internal spaces, case folding, `ParseError` type/attribute/message.
- Unit tests for `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries` (each filter alone and combined, inclusive bounds, empty input).
- CLI tests calling `cli.main(argv)` with captured stdout/stderr and temp files, plus at least one subprocess test of `python -m pennywise` with stdin `-`. Cover every command, `--json`, exit codes 0/1/2, `add` leaving the file untouched on error and creating a missing file, and the examples in the brief verbatim.
- A packaging check: `pip install .` into a fresh venv provides `import pennywise` and the `pennywise` command.

## Out of Scope

- Third-party dependencies, export formats other than CSV, editing/deleting entries, currencies, budgets, config files.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` (Python ≥3.9, no third-party deps) provides `import pennywise` and a `pennywise` console command.
- [ ] `parse(text)` returns entries in file order with `.date` (date), `.category` (lower-case str), `.amount` (Decimal), `.note` (str, `""` if none); fields split on any spaces/tabs; note is the trimmed rest of the line.
- [ ] Amounts accept an optional sign and at most two decimals (`12`, `+2500`, `12.5`, `-0.99`); reject `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`.
- [ ] Blank lines and `#` lines are ignored; any other bad line (incl. impossible dates like `2024-02-30`) raises `pennywise.ParseError` (a `ValueError`) with `.line` = 1-based line number and a message containing `line N`.
- [ ] `balance` (Decimal, 0 when empty), `by_category`, `by_month` (`"YYYY-MM"` keys) and `filter_entries` (case-insensitive category, inclusive `since`/`until`, input order kept) behave as specified.
- [ ] `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals.
- [ ] `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints `name  total` lines sorted by name (default by category).
- [ ] `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since D] [--until D]` prints `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT[ NOTE]`, oldest first, same-day file order kept.
- [ ] `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` appends (creating the file if needed) and prints the added line in `list` format; an invalid entry exits 1 and leaves the file exactly as it was.
- [ ] `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order.
- [ ] `--json` on `balance`, `summary`, `list` prints the specified JSON with two-decimal string amounts.
- [ ] `-` as FILE reads stdin for every reading command.
- [ ] Exit codes: 0 success; 1 ledger/entry mistake with a stderr message naming the line and empty stdout; 2 unreadable file or bad command line (no/unknown command, bad option value, mistyped date).
- [ ] The brief's three CLI examples produce exactly the shown output.

## Original request

EOF
